newsitem.title: UK: Debt traders frown at Bulgaria, smile on Russia.
newsitem.headline: Debt traders frown at Bulgaria, smile on Russia.

text.p: Bulgaria got a fresh battering on the emerging debt market on Thursday but, for a brief moment, Russian paper hit a new high in a market which is generally firm but on tenterhooks as it awaits U.S. payrolls figures.

Bulgarian debt prices have plunged this week on growing fears that its economy could be heading for disaster after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) delayed payment of the August tranche of a loan.
"The whole country story is extremely weak and worrying. Just because it is cheap doesn't mean it can't get cheaper," West Merchant Bank economic adviser Peter West said.

The price of Bulgarian Brady bonds -- commercial debt on which the country defaulted and two years ago restructured into new bonds -- has slumped more than 11 percent since the middle of August and over 20 percent since the start of the year.
The Brady bond market, one of the most active markets in emerging economies, developed at the end of the 1980s after the huge debts of leading Latin American borrowers began to be restructured.
The concept, proposed by former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, later spread to the transition economies of Eastern Europe, including Poland and Bulgaria.
Analysts have increasingly warned of the dangers that Bulgaria could default next year when it has some $1.4 billion in foreign debt service payments.
But some say the chances of the IMF pulling the rug from under Bulgaria are remote and that the debt's enormous yield compared to the rest of the market keeps it an attractive buy.
"I like it. It will not default...it's not a positive credit story but if you don't think it will default, why not hold it," said Bank of America senior trader Michael Jordan.
He pointed to current yields on the debt of up to 15 percent while spreads over U.S. Treasuries are more than 1,500 basis points.
By delaying payment, the IMF was ensuring that when it did provide the money, Bulgaria would use it to service its Brady bonds and not for some other purpose, he added.

"We think that the government will again give in to the IMF and finally receive the next loan," CS First Boston said in its weekly update. "But this would not offer a solution in the long term as an increase in the VAT (value added tax) would fuel further the existing inflationary spiral."
Russian debt briefly hit a new high in early trading at 63-1/4 cents of face value, though it quickly dropped back.
Traders noted market rumours that a U.S. fund had decided to increase its Russia allocation and said there was no particular fresh news out of Russia to lend support.
However, creditor approval to restructure about $32 billion of debt which Russia took on after the collapse of the Soviet Union into new loans is all but certain, traders said.

One creditor source, involved in the rescheduling negotiations, said the process of settling the debt appeared to be going ahead without any hitches, though at a rather slow pace, with a deal expected to be closed by the end of this year.
A key attraction for investors at the moment is Russia's impending Eurobond issue, planned for November, which should help to bring up Russian debt prices even further.

The rest of the emerging debt market is firm, though few traders are prepared to do much ahead of Friday's U.S. non-farm payrolls data which is expected to signal whether U.S. interest rates are headed for a rise.
The West Merchant Bank index for the Brady market is almost back to its end-August peak and, at 156.28, very close to an all-time high of 160.89 reached on January 13, 1994.
